by Terephthalonitrile: Entry to Trisubstituted Allenes

ABSTRACT: An electroreduction method for regioselective 1,4-hydro(deutero)arylation of 1,3-enynes with aryl iodides and H
2
O
or D
2
O has been developed, delivering diverse aryl-functionalized trisubstituted allenes under mild, transition-metal-free, and
external reductant-free conditions. Upon the activation of terephthalonitrile as the organic electron transfer mediator, the protocol
enables the formation of aryl radicals via single-electron transfer (SET) reduction with aryl iodides. The protocol shows a broad
substrate scope with a good functional group compatibility and allows deuterium labeling using D
2
O with up to 99% D-
incorporation. Mechanistic studies support a cathodic radical anion−single electron reduction−cathodic radical polar crossover relay
pathway, offering a sustainable approach to access trisubstituted allenes.
T
he regioselective functionalization of π-conjugated
systems remains a central pursuit in modern synthetic
chemistry, offering strategic routes to construct value-added
architectures from simple and readily available precursors.
Among these systems, 1,3-enynes, which are composed of
conjugated alkene and alkyne moieties, serve as highly versatile
synthons for the construction of complex molecules in
synthesis.
1−3
In particular, the 1,4-hydrofunctionalization of
1,3-enynes has emerged as a powerful strategy for the direct
construction of diverse functionalized allenes,
3−7
which are
privileged structural motifs widely found in natural products,
pharmaceuticals, and functional materials and are highly
reactive synthetic intermediates.
8
Conventionally, 1,3-enyne
1,4-hydrofunctionalization approaches, such as hydrosilylation,
hydroborylation, hydroamination, and hydrocarbonylation,
have predominantly relied on the transition-metal catalysts,
such as palladium, rhodium, copper, and nickel (Scheme
1A).
3,4
While these methods have achieved remarkable levels
of reactivity and selectivity, they often require the use of highly
expensive transition metals and stoichiometric external
reductants and/or may generate toxic byproducts. Recently,
radical-mediated 1,3-enyne 1,4-hydrofunctionalizations have
been extensively developed, providing access to a wide range of
functionalized allenes (Scheme 1B).
6,7
These reactions
typically proceed through photoredox, electrochemical, or
nickel reductive catalysis to generate radicals, followed by
radical addition to the enyne, single-electron reduction, and
subsequent protonation. For example, the 1,4-hydroalkylation
of 1,3-enynes with alkyl bromides or alkyl N-hydroxyphthali-
mide (CONHPI) esters involves single-electron transfer
(SET) reduction of the alkyl halide by Ni(0) or Ni(I),
generating alkyl radicals that furnish trisubstituted allenes via a
nickel-catalyzed reductive radical−polar crossover (RPC)
pathway (Scheme 1B-b).
7
Despite that radical-mediated 1,4-
hydrofunctionalizations such as hydroborylation, hydro-
(deutero)silylation, hydrofluoromethylation, and hydrophos-
phinylation have been well established, the 1,4-hydroarylation
of 1,3-enynes to access highly valuable aryl-substituted allenes,
to the best of our knowledge, remains unexplored.
6
Addition-
ally, the pursuit of greener alternatives continues to drive the
development of transition-metal-free radical chemistry, which
opens new avenues for modular allene synthesis, while
overcoming key limitations of traditional metal-catalyzed
protocols in terms of sustainability, cost, and functional
group compatibility.
Driven by this goal, we initiated our investigation into the
hydroarylation of 1,3-enynes with aryl halides under electro-
chemical conditions (Scheme 1C). Our strategy centers on the
electroreductive generation of aryl radicals via cathodic single-
electron transfer (SET) from aryl halides, facilitated by organic
redox mediators,
9
thereby avoiding the need for metal

catalysts. We surmised that the in situ generated aryl radicals
would undergo selective addition to the distal (alkene) carbon
of 1,3-enyne, forming a short-lived allenyl radical intermediate.
A subsequent SET reduction and protonation of this
intermediate would then deliver the desired allenes with high
regioselectivity. Beyond avoiding transition metals, this
mediated electrolysis strategy offers several key advantages: it
circumvents the high reduction potential of aryl halides,
enabling aryl radical generation under mild electrochemical
conditions, and prevents degradation of sensitive functional
groups often observed under high voltage. Additionally, water
can serve as a benign and abundant proton source, and the
method is readily adaptable to use low-cost and commercially
available D
2
O as a deuterium donor, enabling the efficient
synthesis of deuterium-labeled allenes�molecules of growing
value in pharmaceutical, metabolic, and mechanistic studies.
10
We commenced our study by evaluating optimal conditions
for 1,4-hydroarylation using (3-methylbut-3-en-1-yn-1-yl)-
benzene 1a and 4-iodobenzonitrile 2a as the model substrates
(Table 1). After extensive optimization, we identified effective
conditions that involve a combination of an organic electron
transfer mediator terephalonitrile Med-1, H
2
O (50 equiv) as
the proton source, benzyltrimethylammonium chloride
(BnNMe
3
Cl) as the supporting electrolyte, and MeCN as
the medium in an undivided cell equipped with a zinc cathode
and a graphite felt (GF) anode at 9 mA constant current,
affording the desired allene product 3 in a 65% isolated yield
(entry 1). The results show that the constant current, mediator
Med-1, and BnNMe
3
Cl electrolyte are essential for the
reaction success, as no desired 1,4-hydroarylation reaction
occurred when lacking each (entries 2, 7, and 13).
Replacement of Med-1 by other organic mediators Meds-2−
5 resulted in significantly lower yields or no formation of the
desired product (entries 3−5), further underscoring the
importance of mediator structures. Reducing the Med-1
loading to 10 mol % led to a decreased yield (entry 6).
Other electrolytes, such as BnNEt
3

4

n

NCl,
led to inferior results (entries 8−10). The combination of a
zinc cathode and graphite felt anode along with a constant
current of 9 mA proved optimal, and other electrode materials
or current settings reduced efficiency (entries 11−15). Among
examinations of the solvent effect (such as MeCN, DMF, and
DCM), the results revealed that MeCN was found to be the
best solvent option (entries 1 and 16). Delightedly, the
reaction could be handled with a scale up to 1 mmol 1a,
providing 3 in good yield (entry 17).
After the optimized reaction conditions were established, the
substrate scope of this electrochemical 1,3-enyne 1,4-hydro-
(deutero)arylation protocol was assessed by reaction of a
diverse array of 1,3-enynes 1 with aryl halides 2 in the presence
of H
2
O under the optimized conditions (Table 2). Initially,
various structurally and electronically varied 4-aryl-substituted
1,3-enynes, including electron-rich and electron-deficient aryl-
substituted ones, were examined and showed high reactivity for
this electrochemical 1,3-enyne 1,4-hydroarylation, affording
allenes 4−18 in moderate to good yields. A wide range of
functionalities, including Me,
t
Bu, MeO, CF
3
, F, Cl, and Br, on
the aryl ring at the terminal alkyne were well tolerated (4−13).
Especially, halo groups such as F, Cl, and Br remained intact
during the hydroarylation process, thereby offing highly
reactive potential handles for further derivatizations. Notably,
4-aryl 1,3-enynes bearing a Br group at the para, meta, and
ortho position, respectively, underwent the 1,4-hydroarylation
smoothly, affording 10 and 12−13 in good yields. The results
indicated that the steric hindrance did not affect the reaction,
and the reaction might be applicable to aryl bromides. Indeed,

biphenyl, naphthalene, and thiophene, containing 1,3-enynes,
were also compatible for furnishing allenes 11 and 15−16 in
58−63% yields. Interestingly, 4-alkyl 1,3-enyne was a suitable
substrate, giving 17 in a good yield. The 2,4-diaryl-substituted
1,3-enyne was well tolerated, affording the product in good
yield (18), whereas the 2,4-dialkyl analogue gave no product
(19).
Next, the scope of aryl halides was investigated in the
presence of (3-methylbut-3-en-1-yn-1-yl)benzene 1a, H
2

Med-1, and BnNMe

excellent functional group compatibility: a wide range of
electron-deficient and electron-rich aryl iodides bearing a
functionality, such as CO
2
Me, CF
3
, Cl, Br, Me, MeO, and Ph,
on the aryl ring efficiently manipulated 1,4-hydroarylation with
1,3-enyne 1a, affording 20−26 in moderate to good yields.
Electron-neutral iodobenzene also accommodated this 1,4-
hydroarylation (27). Fortunately, aryl iodides possessing
important naphthalene and thiophene functionalities were
found to be compatible with the optimized conditions, giving
allenes 28−29 in good yields. The regioselectivity and
functional group tolerance of the protocol were further
demonstrated by the successful 1,4-hydroarylation of 1,3-
enynes with a methanol L -moiety (30) or an L -borneo-derived
aryl iodide (31), underscoring the applicability of this method
to construct complex and biologically relevant molecules.
Encouraged by these results, we further extended this
electroreductive strategy to 1,4-deuteroarylation of 1,3-enynes
using terephalonitrile Med-1 as the organic electron transfer
mediator (32−39).

To gain further insight into the reaction mechanism, a series
of control mechanistic experiments were carried out (Scheme
2). The addition of radical scavengers such as TEMPO, BHT,
and hydroquinone completely suppressed allene formation,
suggesting the involvement of radical intermediates in the 1,4-
hydroaryl process. Furthermore, the phenyl radical, generated
from iodobenzene, was successfully trapped by TEMPO, and
the corresponding adduct 40 was detected by high-resolution
mass spectrometry (HRMS), providing direct evidence for aryl
radical formation (Scheme 2A). Cyclic voltammetry (CV)
studies revealed that the reduction potential of iodobenzene is
significantly more negative than that of Med-1, indicating that
Med-1 is preferentially reduced at the cathode (Scheme 2B).

Furthermore, a continuous increase in the catalytic current of
Med-1 was observed upon the addition of iodobenzene,
consistent with a single-electron transfer (SET) process from
the reduction form of Med-1 (dicyanobenzene radical anion)
to the aryl iodide (Scheme 2B).
Based on these observations and the precedent litera-
ture,
1−7,9
a plausible mechanism was proposed as illustrated in
Scheme 2C. Initially, terephthalonitrile Med-1 undergoes SET
reduction at the cathode to generate the terephthalonitrile
radical anion intermediate A.
9
This activated species A then
operates SET reduction with aryl iodide 2 to generate the aryl
iodide radical anion intermediate B, followed by the C−I bond
cleavage to afford the aryl radical C. Chemoselectivity addition
of the aryl radical C across the C�C bond of 1,3-enyne 1
gives rise to the formation of the propargyl radical C and then
the allene radical intermediate D.
6,7,11
Cathodic SET reduction
of the intermediate D delivers the allene carbanion
intermediate D.
5
Finally, protonation of intermediate D with
H
2
O furnishes the desired allene product and the OH
−
ion,
species, which upon protonation by water, furnish the final
allene product.
In summary, we have developed a transition-metal-free
electrochemical strategy for the regioselective electroreductive
1,4-hydro(deutero)arylation of 1,3-enynes with aryl iodides
and H
2
O/D
2
O, enabling efficient access to trisubstituted
allenes under mild conditions. The use of an organic redox
mediator overcomes the high reduction potential of aryl
halides, facilitating aryl radical formation via SET reduction.
The protocol features a broad substrate scope and a high
functional group tolerance, which is compatible with D
2
O,
allowing for the synthesis of deuterium-labeled allenes.
Mechanistic studies support a cathodic radical anion single-
electron-reduction cathodic radical polar crossover relay
pathway, highlighting the potential utilities of this sustainable
and versatile protocol.

Electroreductive 1,4-Hydro(deutero)arylation of 1,3-Enynes Enabled
by Terephthalonitrile: Entry to Trisubstituted Allenes
Boxiong Yang, Ming Hu, Chao Hu,* Fu-Jin Sun,* and Jin-Heng Li*

ABSTRACT: An electroreduction method for regioselective 1,4-hydro(deutero)arylation of 1,3-enynes with aryl iodides and H O
or D O has been developed, delivering diverse aryl-functionalized trisubstituted allenes under mild, transition-metal-free, and
external reductant-free conditions. Upon the activation of terephthalonitrile as the organic electron transfer mediator, the protocol
enables the formation of aryl radicals via single-electron transfer (SET) reduction with aryl iodides. The protocol shows a broad
substrate scope with a good functional group compatibility and allows deuterium labeling using D O with up to 99% D-
incorporation. Mechanistic studies support a cathodic radical anion−single electron reduction−cathodic radical polar crossover relay
pathway, ofering a sustainable approach to access trisubstituted allenes.
